title: The Well of Harrow Glen
premise: Elodie Eastwick, a skeptical urban explorer, arrives in Harrow Glen to map a network of tunnels that appear on no survey and finds a village that has quietly kept an old covenant: every generation, the well beneath the church must be 'counted'—and something below counts back. When the melted bell of 1911 rings across the glen, Elodie realizes her own family name is on the covenant ledger, inherited through a grandmother she never met. As villagers who once ignored her begin watching, waiting, and helping in equal measure, she must decide whether to pay the inherited debt or break it. In the end, Elodie descends into the well during the count and offers the one thing that was never owed—the truth of what her grandmother did to escape—and the thing below accepts the ledger rewritten, sealing the tunnels with Harrow Glen's whole population standing witness.
about_author: Edmund Montrose is the pen name of a former surveyor who spent fifteen years mapping disused infrastructure across northern England before turning to horror. He writes in a converted chapel, where he insists the acoustics are 'merely interesting.'

chapters.title: Unsurveyed Ground
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She arrives in Harrow Glen with LiDAR equipment and a contract to document anomalies near the old churchyard, annoyed by the village's flat, practiced unfriendliness. Her scans return a tunnel system that contradicts every official record. Emotional beat: confident professional curiosity curdling into unease when a villager tells her, kindly, to leave before the season turns.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At dawn she hears the church bell ring—a full, bronze peal—though parish records confirm it was melted for scrap in 1911. The vicar denies hearing anything; the church tower is empty except for dust shaped like long use. Emotional beat: the skeptic's first crack, as she realizes everyone in the village heard it and chose silence.

chapters.title: Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Digging into county archives, she finds a covenant ledger listing families bound to the well, renewed each generation. Her grandmother's name is there—Eastwick, entered in 1948, marked 'departed, debt carried.' Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering she was never a stranger here; inheritance as ambush.

chapters.title: The Kindness of Strangers Who Aren't
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Martha Quill, the shopkeeper. Villagers begin small kindnesses—bread left at her door, tools repaired overnight—that feel like preparation rather than welcome. Martha explains nothing but warns: 'The count wants you presentable.' Emotional beat: belonging offered on terrible terms; warmth with teeth.

chapters.title: What the Tunnels Keep
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She enters the tunnels alone and finds them older than the village, walls scored with tally marks going back centuries, and a chamber beneath the well shaft where the air itself seems to listen. She flees when the marks begin including fresh ones—with her initials. Emotional beat: terror of being already known, already counted.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Confession
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, framed by letters found in the vicarage safe. Her grandmother fled Harrow Glen in 1948 after substituting another family's child into the count, buying her own escape with someone else's bloodline. The substituted line died out; the ledger has been hunting its way back to Eastwick ever since. Emotional beat: grief and fury—inherited guilt without inherited choice.

chapters.title: The Count Approaches
chapters.summary: Martha's POV. Preparations overtake the village: doors painted white, children taught an old rhyme, the empty bell tower swept clean. The count comes at the dark of the moon, and this year the ledger will not accept substitutes. Emotional beat: communal dread, and Martha's quiet decision to help Elodie despite the cost to herself.

chapters.title: Running Ahead of It
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She tries to get her family out—her brother arrives mid-chapter, summoned by a letter he never sent—and they flee along the mapped tunnels, only to find every exit returning them to the glen. The bell rings continuously now, audible from underground. Emotional beat: claustrophobic futility; survival priced beyond their means.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, climax. At the dark of the moon she goes down willingly into the well chamber while the village stands witness above. She offers not blood but testimony: the full truth of her grandmother's substitution, spoken aloud so the ledger can be corrected at its source. The thing below weighs her honesty against the old lie. Emotional beat: courage as radical accountability—paying a debt by telling the truth about it.

chapters.title: After the Ringing Stops
chapters.summary: Shared POV, resolution. The bell falls silent; the tunnels seal themselves behind falling earth; the ledger page bearing Eastwick burns to ash in Elodie's hand. Harrow Glen is freed from the covenant, though some villagers mourn the structure it gave their lives. Elodie stays through spring—not out of obligation, but because belonging, finally, was freely given. Emotional beat: costly peace; inheritance transformed into choice.
